gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 'Smart' in 'Smart Holographic Star & Ocean 5D Projector' means a remote and touch buttons with no app or Wi-Fi (Device Diary on the Topacme, which ibisik names as the same unit sold under other names). The ocean projector with real app, Alexa, Google and Matter control is Govee's H6094 at $69.99, 540 ft², 5 V 2 A 10 W, and it ships without a power adapter.
standout_why: I couldn't open any of the rival pages ChatGPT got. Glarex returned HTTP 429 on four tries. Sientle and Retrowave failed on TLS through both tools, and the Walmart pages (cited 20631755363 and business.walmart.com) showed a bot wall. The cited YouTube page returned only the footer. So I compared against ChatGPT's answer and the result titles. ChatGPT only said the Miraclable card's smart features 'aren't independently verified', and its follow-up question about 'smart projector with app or voice control' shows it never settled the point. None of the titles names an app, a voice assistant or Matter. The Walmart titles give film counts from 1 to 24 but no coverage area and no power draw. The finding is new to that set, but I can't rule out that the unread Glarex, Sientle or Retrowave pages state their control method.
decides: If the shopper means 'smart' literally (app, schedules, Alexa or Google), the generic '5D' film projectors at $14.52–$59.99 don't qualify. They are LED and film-slide night lights controlled by remote. The pick becomes the Govee H6094 Ocean Wave at $69.99 on us.govee.com. Its 540 ft² is the only coverage figure the maker states, and the shopper must supply a 5 V / 2 A USB adapter. If 'smart' is just the listing name and they want the cheapest star-and-ocean effect, a generic film unit does the same job and the budget card stands. The extra money buys app and voice control, not a hologram.

findings.label: What 'smart' control means
findings.value: No Wi-Fi, no app. Touch buttons plus a remote for brightness, color, rotation speed and a 30 / 60 / 120 min sleep timer. No built-in speaker.
findings.source_title: Topacme 5D Projector Review 2026: Should You Buy This? (Device Diary, Sam, 2026-06-28)
findings.note: Reviewer's hands-on description. Device Diary says it is 'standalone'.

findings.label: Light source and image method
findings.value: LED behind an HD lens with rotating film discs. Power is over a USB cable of about 4 ft, with no voltage or watts given.
findings.source_title: Topacme 5D Projector Review 2026: Should You Buy This? (Device Diary)
findings.note: The '5D'/'holographic' label is really an LED and film-slide projector.

findings.label: Coverage, as the reviewer described it
findings.value: Whole ceiling of a 12 × 12 ft bedroom (144 ft²). Less intense at about 15 × 15 ft (225 ft²). Dark room, ceiling up to 12 ft.
findings.source_title: Topacme 5D Projector Review 2026: Should You Buy This? (Device Diary)
findings.note: I converted the room sizes to ft² so they compare with Govee's ft² rating. This is a reviewer's visual estimate, not a measurement, and the maker states no area.

findings.label: Film count as stated
findings.value: 24 films in the article text, while the Amazon listing embedded in the same article says 12
findings.source_title: Topacme 5D Projector Review 2026: Should You Buy This? (Device Diary)
findings.note: Film counts don't line up even within one source. Compare by film count and price together, not by the 'HD'/'4K' wording.

findings.label: Same unit sold under several brands; not holographic
findings.value: Ocean Projector = Topacme = Billhol, with near-identical copy. One Walmart version comes with 3 films. 'Optical projection and physical image films'. Walmart average 2.6/5 from 18 ratings.
findings.note: Named reviewer's judgement. The 2.6/5 figure is ibisik's report, and they gave no URL for the listing.
